title: Despite emergency appeal to Supreme Court, Bruce the dog euthanized in California
description: The dog was deemed "vicious" after multiple biting incidents.
fullText:
Despite a last-minute appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court, a 3-year-old 100-pound Great Pyrenees/German Shepherd mix named Bruce, who had been deemed legally "vicious," was euthanized in California on Wednesday, according to the lawyer for an animal rescue center that had sued to stop the move.

The case involving the imminent execution of a personal pet was a highly unusual, if not unprecedented, appeal to reach the court's emergency docket, which typically sees eleventh-hour pleas in capital cases and urgent disputes over government policy.

The dog was euthanized by Ventura County Animal Services (VCAS) before Justice Elena Kagan, who oversees emergency applications in the Ninth Circuit, could weigh in, attorney Dan Bolton confirmed to ABC News.

'Profoundly corrupt': Trump sued in federal court over selling early access to Truth Social posts

Bolton represents the Santa Paula Animal Rescue Center (SPAR), which had overseen the original adoption of the dog and claimed a contractual interest in its wellbeing.

The animal rescue sought to block the euthanasia mandated by local officials and was joined by the dog's owner, Claire Birgy. The legal saga drew national attention.

Bolton said the local case presented, in his view, important constitutional questions on standing.

Lower courts had tossed out the last-ditch appeals to save Bruce by concluding the animal rescue lacked a concrete interest in the dog's survival sufficient to challenge the dangerousness finding by local authorities.

Federal court blocks another part of Trump mail-in voting executive order

In April, a judge determined Bruce was a "vicious dog" and ordered him euthanized after finding he posed a threat to the public after multiple "vicious" biting incidents.

On its website, Ventura County Animal Services described the incidents and released graphic photos of some of the bite wounds. In one case, in February 2024, VCAS said a male minor was bitten on the lips while walking past Bruce "resulting in severe disfiguring lacerations."

In another incident, from September 2025, a man walking past Bruce, who was tied to a pole outside a CVS, was attacked, resulting in "multiple bite wounds to the knee, chest, and forearm and required sutures," according to VCAS.

In November, a woman was walking in her apartment complex when she was walking past the dog and was bitten on the arm, later requiring surgery and skin grafts, according to VCAS.

Bruce was initially ordered to be euthanized no later than May 15, but that was temporarily delayed by a stay issued by a federal court. The stay was lifted earlier this month.

In a statement on Tuesday, Ventura County Animal Services said: "Decisions involving the humane euthanasia of an animal are difficult and complex.  They require us to balance compassion for animals with our responsibility to protect people and ensure public safety.  Dog bite cases are challenging, and we recognize the strong emotions they can generate within our community."

title: Democrats ‘afraid’ of Jennings as White House press secretary, Sellers says
description: Former South Carolina state Rep. Bakari Sellers (D) on Wednesday quipped that Democrats are “afraid” of fellow CNN political commentator Scott Jennings becoming the next White House press secretary. “...
fullText:
Former South Carolina state Rep. Bakari Sellers (D) on Wednesday quipped that Democrats are "afraid" of fellow CNN political commentator Scott Jennings becoming the next White House press secretary.

"Let me help, Scott," Sellers told other "CNN NewsNight" panelists, including Jennings. "Democrats are afraid of Scott Jennings becoming press secretary. There you go. Now you've got the job."

CNN panelists pressed their fellow political commentator to confirm whether he would replace White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who earlier Wednesday announced that she was leaving her role at the end of the month. Jennings at first answered "no."

"I don't know," he continued. "But I'll tell you this: Karoline Leavitt has been maybe the greatest White House press secretary in the last 30 years, at least. She's been nothing short of brilliant."

Jennings, who previously worked on two campaigns for former President George W. Bush and served as an adviser to Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), has been CNN's primary conservative analyst since 2017. He was reportedly in consideration for the White House press secretary role in 2024 after Trump was elected to a second term.

The commentator commended Leavitt on Wednesday for leaving her White House role to be with her family. The outgoing press secretary returned from maternity leave last month after giving birth to her second child in May.

"But I don't know a single Republican in the country who isn't in awe of and in appreciation of Karoline tonight," he said. "So Godspeed on your journey back to your family."

Leavitt wrote in a Wednesday post on the social platform X that, since her return to the White House, she has "felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary."

She pledged that she would continue to be an advocate for President Trump's MAGA agenda and the Republican Party, adding that Trump asked that she serve as an outside adviser ahead of November's midterms.

Trump was the first to announce Leavitt's departure, writing on Truth Social that her decision was one "I totally understand and respect!"

Leavitt was 27 years old when the president tapped her to be press secretary upon his return to the White House, making her the youngest person to assume the role. She also made history last year when she became the first to serve as White House press secretary while pregnant.

No replacement has yet been announced, something former Trump spokesperson Mike Dubke said he was "very surprised" about.

Leavitt was Trump's fifth press secretary between his two terms, preceded by Sean Spicer, Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders (R), Stephanie Grisham and Kayleigh McEnany.

title: False claims about miscarriage risk from Covid-19 vaccines are spreading online. They use a faulty interpretation of data
description: Numerous studies have shown that Covid-19 vaccines are safe during pregnancy, but Republican lawmakers and Trump administration officials have recently stirred up false and misleading claims that are ...
fullText:
Numerous studies have shown that Covid-19 vaccines are safe during pregnancy, but Republican senators have recently stirred up false and misleading claims that are now spreading on social media.

On Monday, Sens. Ron Johnson of Wisconsin and Rand Paul of Kentucky released a batch of text messages retrieved from Dr. Anthony Fauci's former government phone as part of an investigation into the former health official's leadership and actions during the Covid-19 pandemic – including messages in which he discusses the possible risks and safety of the vaccine during pregnancy.

These messages were a launching pad for the spread of inaccurate data, particularly claims about an 82% risk of miscarriage associated with Covid-19 vaccines. The incorrect figure spread online, including in a since-deleted post by Sen. Ted Cruz.

"This is a well-studied area. We knew this in 2021, that there wasn't an increased risk, and now we have five more years of data. So it's hard to believe we would miss a factor of eight increase in miscarriages," Dr. Kevin Ault, an ob/gyn and president-elect of the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases, told CNN's Erin Burnett on Thursday.

In a ​news release, Johnson references an exchange Fauci had in January 2021, in which he said that a second dose of a Covid-19 vaccine "theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the 1st trimester," as well as a criticism of a study that was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in April 2021.

In that study, researchers used data from a vaccine safety monitoring system to track outcomes for nearly 4,000 women enrolled in the registry who received Covid-19 vaccines in the early months of the rollout. Among them, the researchers identified 827 women who had a "completed pregnancy" — of which 712 were live births, 104 were spontaneous abortions or miscarriages, and 11 were other outcomes.

Initially, the researchers used this data to suggest that Covid-19 vaccines had a 12.6% miscarriage rate: 104 spontaneous abortions out of 827 completed pregnancies. That's comparable with the average miscarriage rate of 10% to 20%, according to the Mayo Clinic.

However, a correction was issued in September 2021 to clarify that there was not enough data to calculate the risk of miscarriage using this particular study. The follow-up time was limited, so outcomes were unknown for the vast majority of participants, and the denominator of 827 completed pregnancies did not sufficiently represent the full sample of nearly 4,000 participants.

Still, that correction has been used to manipulate the study data in a way that significantly misrepresents miscarriage risk associated with Covid-19 vaccinations.

The researchers note that 700 of the completed pregnancies were in their third trimester when the mother was vaccinated, and they say that "any risk estimate would need to account for gestational week-specific risk of spontaneous abortion." This meant "no denominator was available to calculate a risk estimate for spontaneous abortions."

But in their claims about the risks of vaccination, critics are instead inaccurately constricting the denominator to exclude those 700 completed pregnancies in the third trimester. This would lead to an overestimation of miscarriage risk of 82%, based on a faulty calculation of 104 spontaneous abortions out of 127 pregnancies completed in the first or second trimester.

Experts in public health and pregnancy care emphasize that the benefits that the Covid-19 vaccine offers pregnant moms — and their babies — significantly outweigh any risk.

"It is without question that the benefits of the vaccine outweigh the risks, and the world's literature on this topic includes hundreds of thousands of women," said Dr. Brenna Hughes, chair of the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine's Infectious Disease and Emerging Threats Committee.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention cites dozens of studies on its website that come to the same conclusion.

"COVID-19 vaccination before and during pregnancy did not increase health risks for pregnant women or their babies," the agency says. "In addition, studies have also shown that COVID-19 vaccination during pregnancy provides protection to both the pregnant woman and the baby."

Hughes says that miscarriage concerns are common for pregnant women and that doctors are constantly discussing risks and benefits with their patients.

"When we offer any intervention in pregnancy, the first question is: 'Is it safe for me? Is it safe for the baby?'"

With Covid-19 vaccines, the risks she tells people about most are a sore arm and some possible fatigue. The benefits are "incredibly clear," she said, and outcomes are "quite the opposite of what of what some of this misinformation is saying."

Covid-19 infection poses significantly more risk to pregnant women than the vaccines, experts say.

"We had hundreds of maternal deaths in 2021 due to Covid, and we still have severe illnesses, ICU stays, stillbirth, preterm deliveries related to those respiratory diseases," Ault said. "Vaccination during pregnancy reduces the risk of all those things. So if somebody's making decisions on these bad sources of information, that has a real downstream effect on maternal health."

And Hughes says she worries that the resurfacing of misinformation about Covid-19 vaccines may leave pregnant women with broader doubts about other interventions.

"One of the concerns that we're seeing now is that people aren't sure who to trust and who the trusted messenger should be," Hughes said, but medical societies are the most reliable sources of information.

"We are very careful about the science that we put into our guidelines," she said. "We rigorously assess it for quality. We debate it to make sure that we think that the science is strong enough, and it is not one person making a decision or a recommendation. This is a committee of people with decades of expertise on these topics who really carefully look at the literature and ensure that we feel that it's adequate before we make these recommendations."

title: Count Binface gets almost 10,000 votes in Clacton by-election
description: The self-styled intergalactic space warrior finished second to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage.
fullText:
Count Binface has enjoyed his best-ever election performance after receiving almost 10,000 votes and finishing second to Nigel Farage at the Clacton by-election.

The self-styled intergalactic space warrior said he was "1,000 times more popular" when standing against Farage compared to Andy Burnham, after he picked up 95 votes when challenging the now-prime minister in Makerfield in June.

Count Binface received 9,455 votes compared to Farage's 22,239. His 26.9% share of the vote is thought to be the highest ever for a novelty candidate.

He became the leading rival to Farage after the main UK parties boycotted the by-election triggered by the Reform UK leader, amid questions over his finances.

Farage had branded Count Binface the "candidate of the establishment" after claiming supporters of other parties had canvassed for him.

The contest in the Essex constituency saw a record 34 candidates for a Westminster Parliament election, although Farage did not attend the announcement of the result in person, denying Count Binface and others a chance to line-up alongside him in the Clacton Leisure Centre.

This led Count Binface to declare he was "the winning candidate in the room".

Reform UK said Essex Police had advised Farage not to attend the count "due to a credible threat against him".

The BBC has been told the force did not advise any candidate that they should not attend the count.

Count Binface is the satirical alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey, who has specialised in satire and been involved with BBC comedy shows, including The Thick of It and Have I Got News For You.

Harvey has previously stood in four parliamentary elections, including against prime ministers, and two London mayoral elections.

His previous best parliamentary result came in the Richmond and Northallerton vote against Rishi Sunak in the 2024 general election when he received 308 votes - 0.6% of the total share - and finished sixth out of 13 candidates.

The Clacton result was the first time that Count Binface has retained the £500 deposit candidates are required to make to validate their nomination.

It is repaid if a candidate polls more than 5% of the total number of valid votes cast in the constituency.

Nigel Farage returns as MP, winning Clacton by-election that major parties boycotted

Farage's by-election victory won't stop questions about finances

Farage had earlier told supporters at a Reform UK event that he was "damned if I'm going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory, a ringing endorsement of all that I've tried to fight for, and you've tried to fight for, and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".

He then added he would not attend the count as Essex Police had told him about an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result".

Count Binface said he had asked police if was there "any credible threat of a disruption here", adding: "I can tell you they said unequivocally no, it was safe to go ahead."

He also told reporters that hearing the "verdict of the Clactonites was the least I could do".

He added: "All I will say to you is what happens next: let's all meet for part two of the Clacton by-election coming soon to a leisure centre near you."

This remark was a nod to a possible second by-election in Clacton, which could occur as a result of an investigation into Farage by Parliament's standards commissioner.

Farage resigned as an MP last month and stood in the subsequent by-election after facing intense scrutiny over financial support he has received.

The standards commissioner had been investigating Farage from May after the Reform leader did not declare a £5m gift he received from billionaire Reform donor Christopher Harborne before he became an MP.

Farage has argued he did not need to declare the gift, which he described as "unconditional".

The investigation was paused as a result of the by-election and resumed following his return to Parliament.

One possible outcome of a standards investigation is a suspension which triggers a recall petition. This process enables an MP to be removed and a by-election triggered if 10% of eligible registered voters sign a petition.

The other main UK parties are expected to put up a candidate if there is a second by-election.

Independent candidate Marc Wilkinson, who received 11 votes, was not happy with the attention Count Binface received during the campaign.

He said: "I was shocked that all the main parties didn't stand, I was shocked that Reform called the by-election, shocked that all the attention has been on Count Binface, most incredibly shocked by the extent to which the other candidates have been essentially ignored."

title: Salford champions? Millers to spiral? - League Two club-by-club preview
description: BBC Sport correspondents assess the strengths and weaknesses of all 24 teams competing in League Two this season.
fullText:
League Two never fails to provide gripping entertainment right until the final day of the season.

If recent years are anything to go by, the 2026-27 campaign promises to be no different with Salford City tipped to win promotion to League One for the first time in their history and York City back in the EFL after a 10-year hiatus.

With Saturday's curtain-raiser upon us, BBC Sport spoke to correspondents across England and Wales for their takes on the clubs they cover and what to expect this season.

Follow your League Two club this 2026-27 season

Andy Bayes, BBC Radio Lancashire

Key ins: Joe Anderson (Barrow, undisclosed), Cole Stockton (Salford, free), Tom Moore (Southport, undisclosed), Louie Moulden (Norwich, loan)

Key outs: Ollie Wright (loan spell ended)

What are the expectations heading into the season? To achieve more points and a higher league position than they did last season. They made a three-point improvement year-on-year last season and flirted with the play-off places in early 2026 before injuries and squad depth took their toll.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? They have strengthened their forward line with the arrival of Cole Stockton, which has to help. Stanley will be hoping that he can return to the form that made him a wanted man during his days at Morecambe.

They have also brought players in from non-league football who will be hungry to show that they belong in the EFL. The club always has a 'never say die' attitude. They are always tipped for relegation in whichever league they play at the start of a season. That's of no interest to manager John Doolan or his squad.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? Injuries and perhaps in some areas a little bit of inexperience could hamper them.

There are key players in the Stanley team that Doolan needs to get 35-plus games from this season - Shaun Whalley being a case in point. He missed the start of last season and was missed badly.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Shaun Whalley. Stanley's results with Whalley in the side are far different to when he isn't. He's a vastly experienced, talented player who his team-mates respect greatly. If he can stay fit for most of the season, they'll be fine.

Key ins: Oisin Gallagher (Lincoln City, loan), Matthew Cox (Brentford, loan)

Key outs: Ryan Glover (Stockport County, undisclosed), Callum Stead (Cambridge United, undisclosed)

What are the expectations heading into the season? Barnet were back in the EFL for the first time in seven years last season and finished eighth, just outside the play-off places. So minimum expectation is the play-offs, although the Bees have never been promoted via that route.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? The manager, Dean Brennan. No matter what the changes or challenges, he never leaves anyone in doubt about his aims or expectations. Plus defensive rock and leader Danny 'Mr Dependable' Collinge.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? The loss of some big players, plenty of new signings, and the need for those new additions to gel quickly with the team. Barnet have one of the smallest budgets, so Brennan's knowledge of non-league is crucial.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Tenacious, highly-skilled pass master Nnamdi Ofoborh is the conductor. Idris Kanu is the creator. Academy graduate Bright Siaw looks an exciting prospect.

Richard Hoskin, BBC Radio Bristol

Key ins: Kofi Balmer (Motherwell, free), Bobby Kamwa (Newport County, undisclosed), Reiss-Alexander Russell-Denny (Tottenham, loan), Tommy Leigh (Bradford City, loan), Richie Smallwood (Tranmere Rovers, free)

Key outs: Isaac Hutchinson (Doncaster Rovers, undisclosed), Kamil Conteh (Bromley, undisclosed)

What are the expectations heading into the season? Rovers ended last season so strongly under Steve Evans that supporters will be hoping to carry that momentum into the new campaign.

It's not gone unnoticed that a number of national pundits and publications are tipping Rovers for automatic promotion – and while a top-three finish is the expectation of most, experienced supporters will want the season to settle down before making any committed predictions.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? A number of players drafted in last January have returned to the club – Kofi Balmer, Tommy Leigh and Richie Smallwood. Defensively Rovers are strong, with a lot of players boasting previous promotions on their CVs.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? There's nothing drastically weak about Bristol Rovers. Some supporters have pointed out that the squad would benefit from the addition of a wide man, but that could well be addressed by the end of the transfer window.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? I've yet to see him play – but recent arrival Reiss-Alexander Russell-Denny could be a key addition to the squad. He'll be keen to emulate the impact of Yusuf Akhamrich, who had a successful loan spell from Tottenham last season.

Steve Kitchen, BBC Radio Gloucestershire

Key ins: Andreas Weimann - among a number of players with higher league experience.

Key outs: Bristol Rovers loanee - Isaac Hutchinson. He scored 15 goals in League Two, finishing with 18 goals in all competitions.

What are the expectations heading into the season? To build on the foundations that manager Steve Cotterill put in place last season. The 2025-26 campaign was about survival, with 18th place a fantastic achievement in the end. Many fans are talking about top half, with a shot at the play-offs if things click.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? After returning to Whaddon Road, with the club favourites for relegation last season, Cotterill reshaped the squad with contacts and hard work on the training ground. Cotterill brought the previously bewildered fans back on side, trusting and backing the manager and his players. That work continues this season with what looks to be a stronger, deeper squad.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? Until the signing of Andreas Weimann, there was a lack of attacking experience alongside an exciting group of younger players looking to learn and strengthen their careers. Cheltenham will need them to settle quickly to life in League Two whilst finding the net, but it now looks like a well balanced squad on the available budget.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? It's easy to say Weimann but in reality there is no 'one player'. The key to Cheltenham's success will be Cotterill and tune that he gets out of a group of players that have joined the club because they've either played for him before, or have been enthused by what he's sold them.

From the kit design to the nets in the goals, he's involved in everything that happens at the club. It's no accident that he was (long overdue) given the keys to the Borough at the end of last season.

League Two fixtures: Your club-by-club guide to the 2026-27 season

Barnet 'better equipped' for promotion, says Brennan

Cheltenham sign striker Weimann on free transfer

Paul Fisher, BBC Radio Sheffield

Last season: 6th (lost in play-off semi-finals)

Key ins: Junior Eccleston (Sutton United, undisclosed), George McEachran (Grimsby Town, free), Jack Simpson (Leyton Orient, free), Alfie Pond (Wolverhampton Wanderers, free), Remeao Hutton (Gillingham, free), Fraser Bryden (Crusaders, undisclosed)

Key outs: Bailey Hobson (Harrogate Town, free), Armando Dobra (Leyton Orient, undisclosed), Jamie Grimes (Boston United, free), Janoi Donacien (Northampton Town, free)

What are the expectations heading into the season? Paul Cook has improved the Spireites in every single season he has managed the club, including the first time he was at Chesterfield just under 14 years ago.

Last season was disappointing that they could not reach the top three despite being tipped by many. This time, Cook and the fans expect promotion.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? Defensively they looked to have strengthened, adding youth to experience, and pace up front will also hopefully be to their benefit.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? Chesterfield conceded the most goals of any team in the top eight last season and still reached the play-offs. If they shore up at the back, top three will be achievable, injuries apart.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Liam Mandeville led Chesterfield's overall assists last season and was second in the table for League Two. If he's on song, then he could do it again.

Key ins: Sean Raggett (Rotherham, free), Thimothee Lo-Tutala (Hull City, loan), Bradley Ihionvien (Peterborough United, laon)

Key outs: Kyreece Lisbie (Reading, undisclosed), Arthur Read (York City, free), Matt Macey (Wycombe Wanderers, free)

What are the expectations heading into the season? It's difficult to know exactly what to expect from Colchester United this season. The previous campaign ended with anticipation of a takeover being completed over the summer, but those plans collapsed in June.

Chairman and owner Robbie Cowling insists a competitive budget was always in place should the sale not happen, but it's not the renewed investment many supporters had hoped for.

Even so, Danny and Nicky Cowley have guided the U's to the fringes of the League Two play-off places in each of the past two seasons and have consistently recruited smartly within their means. If they can continue that trend, Colchester should again be capable of challenging in the top half and pushing for a play-off spot.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? Colchester's summer recruitment looks sensible and solid. Sean Raggett and Paul Digby bring experience, leadership and physicality, while goalkeeper Thimothee Lo-Tutala arrives after a season playing League One football with Doncaster Rovers.

Perhaps more importantly, the U's have retained several key players. Highly rated left-back Ellis Iandolo has committed his future to the club, while influential midfielder Jack Payne remains. Last season's standout performers Jack Tucker and Harry Anderson have also stayed put, giving the squad valuable continuity.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? The biggest concern is a loss of pace and attacking threat in wide areas. Kyreece Lisbie's sale to Reading, coupled with the departures of Owura Edwards and Samson Tovide following the expiry of their contracts, has left gaps to fill.

Former players Bradley Ihionvien and Oscar Thorn have returned on loan deals, providing some familiarity and attacking options. However, Colchester will need to find goals from within the squad quickly if they are to mount a sustained challenge near the top end of the table.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Jack Payne remains Colchester's chief creative force. Operating in the number 10 role, he scored 13 goals last season, including two hat-tricks, and continues to be one of the most effective attacking midfielders in League Two.

What are the expectations heading into the season? Until Tranmere Rovers' takeover is completed, it's difficult to say exactly what the club's aims are. The situation off the pitch is far from ideal, with supporters growing increasingly frustrated.

On the pitch, Tranmere have finished in a lower league position in each of the past seven seasons since their relegation to League Two in 2020. They've been dangerously close to the relegation places in the past two seasons, including last year's great escape under Pete Wild when they survived on the final day.

With Darrell Clarke now in charge, Tranmere should be looking up and their EFL Cup performance against Rochdale showed plenty of positives for the squad to take forward. Overall, the aim will likely be to avoid any concerns of the drop this campaign.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? This squad has goals in it and it will need them to make up for Omari Patrick's departure.

Charlie Whitaker and Jordan Davies both scored in the EFL Cup preliminary round defeat by Rochdale, while there'll be a huge emphasis on former Watford winger Tom Ince after his surprise move to Prenton Park.

Joe Ironside is a proven forward at League Two level despite an underwhelming first season and defender Nathan Smith scored more goals than any other centre-back in the division last year.

Of course, they then have to keep goals out at the back but there is potential for exciting, attacking football this season.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? To put it simply, struggling to win football matches. In each of the past two seasons, only two teams have won less games than Tranmere Rovers in League Two and three of those four teams were relegated with the exception of Crawley who finished 22nd last season.

Despite a huge turnover in the squad between the two campaigns, that trend has continued which is undoubtedly a big concern. That's something that must change under Clarke if Tranmere are to progress.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? It has to be Ince. His arrival on a free transfer is a massive coup and statement of intent.

This is only the second season of his career that he's played outside the top two divisions of English football, the other being a loan spell at Notts County in League One in 2010-11.

He brings a wealth of experience and quality to the club, having played in the Championship for each of the past four seasons. He even scored a league hat-trick for Watford last season against Birmingham City. He'll be relied upon to be a leader on and off the pitch.

Key ins: James Connolly (Crewe Alexandra, free), Sven Sprangler (St Johnstone, undisclosed), Andy Dallas (Barnsley, free)

Key outs: Jamille Matt (released), Aden Flint (released), Brandon Comley (Barnet, free), Josh Gordon, Priestley Farquharson (Crawley Town, free), Connor Barrett (Wigan Athletic, undisclosed), Evan Weir (Peterborough United, free), Jamie Jellis (Rotherham, free), Charlie Lakin (Barnet, free)

What are the expectations heading into the season? Lee Grant's own expectations appear high. Supporters would be justified in being more guarded, and may remain so for some time even if the club starts well after the bruising experiences of the past two seasons.

But last week's win at Bristol City in the EFL Cup, with a performance that demonstrated organisation and energy – always a good early sign under a new manager – may raise sights.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? The early signs are that the strength may be in the collective.

The switch of formation from the 4-2-3-1 of pre-season to a back three at Ashton Gate appears less significant than the apparent ease of the players in adapting to it, with their smooth organisation a feature. If sustained, Walsall could be more productive than the sum of their parts may suggest.

Although they are short on well-known names at this level, especially with Alex Pattison out of the picture for a while, there are several young players – Mason Hancock, Harrison Burke and Courtney Clarke among them – with clear potential to move their careers forward if this season goes well. If fitter for longer, Aaron Pressley can be an effective spearhead.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? Like all teams with a young core in such a closely-fought league, progress may not always follow a steady upward gradient.

Some of their talented youngsters will prove themselves at this level, others will stumble, and it is not always easy to predict which. Their squad is also small enough at present to come under pressure – not only to protect against injuries, but also uneven form.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Courtney Clarke took a more scenic route to regular professional football than most with his talent, via South Shields and Eastbourne before his chance with the Saddlers.

His first full season at League Two level was up and down, and his longest run of league starts was only five. But there were enough examples of his ability – explosive bursts of speed from various parts of midfield and a spectacular goal at Norwich – to believe that with a year in the league behind him, he can start to produce those moments more often.

New EFL season gets under way... for four teams

York striker Stones signs five-year deal

York appoint Lindsey after shock Maynard sacking

Last season: National League champions (promoted)

Key ins: Scott Lindsey (head coach), Arthur Read (Colchester United, free)

Key outs: Stuart Maynard (head coach)

What are the expectations heading into the season? Until a couple of weeks ago, supporters were expecting a tilt at promotion with the owners openly admitting that if City didn't go back-to-back, they will have failed this season.

However, if they don't get off to a good start, the pressure will soon increase on new head coach Scott Lindsey and those in charge. Has a football club where there is disharmony in the background, ever been successful on the pitch?

After a summer of huge optimism, part-owner Matt Uggla's decision to sack Stuart Maynard, and not really explain why, has completely destroyed the positive atmosphere around City's return to the EFL for the first time in 10 years.

With rumours some players who were part of City's record-breaking squad not being happy with the change, how long will it take them to get over the shock of it?

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? The togetherness of the many players that remain from last season and the bond they have with supporters. They'll always give 100% irrespective of what they think about some of the decisions made in the past couple of weeks.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? Having to get used to a new system and a manager not knowing how to get the best out of the players he has inherited.

Brought in just a couple of weeks before the start of City's return to the EFL, can Lindsey get the players to reach the same dizzy heights Maynard got them to last season?

Of course it's not Lindsey's fault Maynard was sacked, but that didn't stop chants of "you're getting sacked in the morning" and "Stuart Maynard's Barmy Army" coming down from the stands during the EFL Cup defeat by Crawley. If City don't get off to a flying start in League Two, they are likely to get louder.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Striker Josh Stones. Superb last season. The £300,000 signing from Wigan 18 months ago has already been attracting admiring advances from other clubs.

But he's now signed a new long-term contract. However, if the goals start to flow, he'll be the next player to leave the LNER for a huge transfer fee.

title: Machado Garry heavily booed at UFC 330 news conference
description: Ian Machado Garry says fans will be chanting his name when he beats welterweight champion Islam Makhachev at UFC 330 after they relentlessly boo him at a news conference in Philadelphia.
fullText:
Ian Machado Garry said fans will be chanting his name when he beats welterweight champion Islam Makhachev at UFC 330 after he was relentlessly booed at a news conference in Philadelphia.

The Irishman was booed as soon as he was introduced to the stage, with fans pledging their allegiance to Russia's Makhachev, who is looking to further cement his legacy on Saturday.

"On Saturday night that belt will be wrapped around my waist and every single one of you is going to change - it's going to be 'let's go Garry' chants," Machado Garry said.

"I couldn't care less [about the booing]. My little boy is here laughing and making faces - I'm living the dream.

"I get to fight for a world title. I dreamt of this room when I was a 16-year-old kid and this weekend all of my dreams come true. Nobody can take that away from me."

Machado Garry, 28, has a record of 17 wins in 18 professional bouts and has 10 wins from 11 fights since signing with the UFC to emerge as the number one contender in the welterweight division.

Machado Garry told reporters during Wednesday's media day that he would only be answering questions about the fight, and he shut down one of those journalists, who he felt overstepped the mark, during Thursday's news conference.

The journalist in question said: "A lot of fans sometimes say that Ian is annoying, do you find Ian annoying?", but Machado Garry interjected before Makhachev could answer.

"That's a loaded question," Machado Garry said.

"What you're doing now is trying to cause trouble. We're friends, I thought we were cool. That's putting words in his mouth and you know it.

"If he thinks that he can be honest and say it, but your job as a journalist is to be professional and stick to the sport.

"This is the biggest fight of the year, I think there are more important things to talk about."

Machado Garry said he felt "nervous energy" from Makhachev when they faced off in front of the iconic Rocky Balboa statue on Wednesday.

But it was very cordial when they came face-to-face on Thursday, shaking hands before Machado Garry said "you ready?"

Regarded by many as one of the greatest MMA fighters of all time, Makhachev, 34, vacated his lightweight title in January 2025 after four successful defences and claimed the welterweight belt in November.

He has lost just once in his 29 fight career - winning 17 of his 18 contests in the UFC - with his sole defeat coming in 2015.

"Beating him proves I'm special," Machado Garry said.

"Everyone of you fans consider him to be the number one pound-for-pound fighter on the planet, you consider him to be the greatest martial artist walking the earth.

"When I beat him, you'll all shut your mouth and think I'm great."

Victory will see Makhachev move clear of Anderson Silva's 16 successive wins in the UFC - a record which has stood for 13 years.

Earlier in the week, Makhachev said he "does not have much time" left in the UFC but at the news conference he appeared to suggest he could be around for a while to come.

"Seventeen [wins] is not going to be enough. I want to be sure that nobody breaks my record so it needs to be 20 minimum," Makhachev said.

"Let's talk about the GOAT numbers after my career. I'm still winning. After my 20-win streak then let's talk."

There is also a title on the line in Saturday's co-main event with Gillian Robertson facing strawweight champion Mackenzie Dern.

Canada's Robertson has been with the UFC since 2017 and is getting her first shot at a belt in her 21st fight with the promotion.

The 31-year-old, who holds the record for most submission wins (7) in UFC history, repeated claims that she has been disrespected by American Dern all week.

"She has been diminishing my skills throughout the media, saying she doesn't know what belt I am or who I am, but she's chasing the submission record which I have," Robertson said.

Dern beat Virna Jandiroba to claim the vacant belt in October and has six submission wins on her record in the UFC.

"It feels like we're in high school, like 'who doesn't like each other', but the best time we'll get to know each other is in the octagon for 25 minutes," Dern responded.

title: Brewery sells three pubs to 'stabilise' business
description: Venues in Sheffield and Barnsley will be sold to "strengthen and stabilise" the overall business.
fullText:
An independent brewery and hospitality operator has agreed the sale of three of its pubs.

True North Brew Co has given up The British Oak in Mosborough and The Old Grindstone in Crookes, both in Sheffield, along with The Milton Arms in Elsecar, Barnsley.

The company said it wanted to "strengthen and stabilise" its business due to a "challenging period" for the industry.

Owner Kane Yeardley, said: "This has not been an easy decision, but it is a necessary step to secure the long-term future of our company. We are committed to supporting our teams through this transition and ensuring our remaining venues continue to thrive."

The company, which acquired the Abbeydale Picture House in Sheffield in 2025 to transform it into a "premier entertainment venue", said the three pubs had been "an important part of the company's estate".

It said it had relinquished them to secure new ownership that would continue to operate them as pubs, "preserving their character and role" within their local communities.

In 2024, The Waggon and Horses in Sheffield was given a new lease to use a nearby park as its beer garden after True North Brew went into administration in 2023.

Administrators had sold its assets to new owners Cocktails and Craft Beers Ltd and all jobs were saved.

According to Companies House records, in 2023 the new owners successfully applied to change their name to True North Brew Co.

In April, plans were approved for the brewery to convert part of Grade II-listed Walkley Library in Sheffield to include a cafe-bar.

The company said while deciding to sell the three pubs it took a "considered and proactive approach" to protect the long-term health of its wider estate, focusing on "preserving the strength" of the core business.

Is said the sale and transfer was expected to complete within about three months and it remained "fully committed" to supporting the wellbeing and future of its employees.

All affected team members would have the opportunity to transfer to the new owners, it said. For those who wanted to remain with True North Brew Co, every effort would be made to find suitable alternative opportunities within the business.

The company thanked its staff and customers for their "continued support, loyalty, and dedication".

title: HHS warns Texas hospitals against denying life-saving care to newborn with disability
description: HHS warned Children's Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern they cannot withhold treatment from baby Gabriel based on his heart defect.
fullText:
The Trump administration is stepping into the battle over a Texas newborn with a severe heart defect, warning two hospitals they cannot withhold medical treatment because of his disability.

The Department of Health and Human Services' Office for Civil Rights told Fox News Digital Thursday it is sending a letter to Children's Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern Medical Center outlining their obligations under federal disability civil rights laws as doctors make treatment decisions involving baby Gabriel.

The federal intervention comes after Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton took action to ensure the newborn receives medically necessary care after a dispute that began when his biological parents allegedly asked their surrogate to abort him after he was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome.

Surrogate Gives Birth In Texas To Baby With Heart Defect After Parents Requested Abortion

Surrogate mother McKenna West refused the request and traveled to Texas, where Gabriel was born Wednesday and taken to a neonatal intensive care unit.

In its letter, HHS' civil rights office makes clear that federal law prohibits withholding medical treatment based on a person's disability, including based on judgments that the life of someone with a disability has less value or that the individual would impose a burden on others.

Those federal protections extend to decisions involving life-sustaining treatment, according to HHS.

The agency said it is monitoring Gabriel's case and offering technical assistance to Children's Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern as the hospitals determine his care.

Hhs Official Warns Of Irreversible Risks As Trump Admin Restricts Funding For Youth Gender Procedures

HHS is also urging the hospitals to seek a review by an infant care committee if doctors consider withholding or withdrawing medically indicated treatment. The agency said life-sustaining treatment should continue during that review.

The federal action marks the latest intervention in the dispute over Gabriel's medical care.

West was around 20 weeks pregnant when Gabriel was diagnosed with hypoplastic left heart syndrome, a congenital condition in which the left side of the heart is severely underdeveloped. The diagnosis allegedly prompted the intended parents to ask West to have an abortion, according to Paxton's office.

West instead traveled to Texas, and Paxton formally notified UT Southwestern Medical Center and Children's Medical Center of Dallas of what his office said were their legal obligations to provide Gabriel with "medically necessary, life-saving care upon birth."

Texas Ag Paxton Demands Dallas Sheriff Pursue Ice Agreement As Deadline Dispute Sparks Legal Threat

Paxton later secured a court order aimed at ensuring the baby received care after birth.

"The court has made the right decision in immediately acting to protect baby Gabriel's life and ensure he receives the care he deserves," Paxton said.

"My office utilized every tool at our disposal to protect life, and we will not back down in continuing to support baby Gabriel's well-being," he added. "Every child in our state deserves to be cared for and protected, and that's exactly what I'll fight for."

The case has drawn an outpouring of support for West from conservative and pro-life advocates, who praised her decision to continue the pregnancy and fight for Gabriel's care.

Supreme Court Unanimously Slaps Down Blue State Targeting Pro-life Group

Andrew Kolvet, a spokesman for Turning Point USA, called West a "hero" on X, writing that she "saved this baby's life" and saying he hopes she is ultimately able to keep Gabriel.

Alliance Defending Freedom, which represents West, celebrated the court order requiring Gabriel to receive the surgery. ADF Senior Counsel Erik Baptist praised West's "courageous stand" for Gabriel and said "every child deserves a chance at life."

Pro-life group Live Action also praised West for resisting pressure to abort Gabriel but said the fight is not over. The group raised concerns that a court order is preventing West from having contact with the newborn, saying Gabriel "needs the comfort of the only mother he's ever known" and that his needs should remain the priority.

Gabriel was born Wednesday and transported to a neonatal intensive care unit, where doctors could perform surgery to treat his heart condition.

"Baby Gabriel deserves a chance at life, and I will not allow anyone to unlawfully deny him medically necessary care," Paxton previously said. "My office will use every tool available to protect innocent lives and ensure that every child receives the care required under Texas law."

Fox News Digital reached out to Children's Medical Center of Dallas and UT Southwestern Medical Center for comment.

Fox News Digital's Robert McGreevy contributed to this report.
