title: Vance to GOP: Don’t blame young people for being sympathetic to socialism
description: Vice President Vance issued a warning to Republicans on Thursday about the momentum of progressive candidates on the left, saying GOP members can only blame themselves if they don’t persuade young vot...
fullText:
Vice President Vance issued a warning to Republicans on Thursday about the momentum of progressive candidates on the left, saying GOP members can only blame themselves if they don't persuade young voters.

"Our response to that [socialism] can't just be to ignore the economic concerns that I think are feeding this rising interest in socialism," Vance said in an interview with Fox News's "The Will Cain Show."

"You as an American citizen deserve to have a good life in this country, and you deserve to have a government that is making it easier for you to start a family, for you to afford to get a good education, for you to have a good job, for you to afford a home," he continued.

Vance touted the Trump administration's economic policies, noting that "these things sometimes take a little bit of time."

The vice president referred to investments into the U.S. leading to middle-class jobs, the stabilization of housing prices and the administration's push to lower interest rates.

"We want people to be able to afford the good things about this wonderful country we all live in," he continued.

"My warning to my fellow Republicans would be if we don't get this right, don't blame young people for being sympathetic to socialism. We've got to blame ourselves," he said. "You don't stop socialism by throwing slogans at people about the free market. As much as I love the free market, you stop socialism by making people's lives better, and that's what we're trying to do every single day."

Vance's comments come amid a rise in progressive candidates in Democratic primaries across the country. President Trump and his allies have adopted the strategy of labeling the candidates and other Democrats by extension as socialists and communists.

However, a slew of recent polls show growing voter dissatisfaction with the administration's handling of the economy. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released earlier this month showed Trump's approval rating falling from 35 percent to 37 percent. It also showed 37 percent said they preferred the Democratic Party's approach to the economy, while 36 percent said they preferred the GOP approach.

title: Hammers & Boro to go up? Championship club-by-club preview
description: BBC Sport correspondents take a closer look at the 24 teams taking part in the 2026-27 Championship season.
fullText:
Here we go again... you can leave the Viking Row, Wonderwall, Mexican ducks and (most) hydration breaks in the summer of '26 - proper football is back.

The open road of the Championship season stretches nine months before us, punctuated by 46 twists and turns along the way.

Whisper it, but it looks like being one of the most open and competitive seasons ever in a division which is already known around the world for being ridiculously unpredictable.

Just four of the 24 clubs in the second tier have the benefit of parachute payments in 2026-27, newly relegated West Ham, Wolves and Burnley, while the other, Southampton, begin the campaign with a four-point penalty after the spygate scandal which cast a shadow over the climax of the last campaign.

Lincoln City take their place in the division for the first time since 1961 after their heroics in League One, while Cardiff bounced back after a 12-month exile as runners-up and Bolton join them in the Championship for the first time since 2019.

As Wolves and Blackburn prepare to hit the open road on Friday, BBC Sport correspondents across England and Wales break down the 24 teams and what - at this stage at least, given the transfer window remains open until 1 September - we can expect from them.

Jobi McAnuff from the BBC's dedicated EFL podcast 72+ also offers his predicted finishes in the table.

Fighting relegation & eyeing promotion? Championship set for six-team play-offs

How will relegated trio fare in the Championship?

Key ins: James Beadle (Brighton, loan), Dael Fry (Middlesbrough), Kristoffer Lund (Palermo), Jhon Solis (Girona), Luis Vazquez (Anderlecht)

Key outs: Kai Wagner (Philadelphia Union), Ibrahim Osman (end of loan), Jonathan Panzo (released), Tommy Doyle (end of loan), Kyogo Furuhashi (LA Galaxy)

Expectations? While many supporters expected play-off places last season, this time around it is a more realistic ambition. Indeed, entering his third season boss Chris Davies will likely accept that the expectation of the owners will be a top eight finish as a minimum.

Strengths? There is a sense of continuity from the second half of last season when the squad was revamped with younger, hungrier players. The likes of winger Carlos Vicente, midfield stopper Jhon Solis and striker August Priske will have all benefited from the experience they gained. Skipper Christoph Klarer and Phil Neumann should be one of the more formidable central defensive pairings in the Championship.

Weaknesses? Any route to the play-offs will require a rethink as to how Chris Davies sets up away from home. Last season they fell short on their travels - their five away wins put them in the Championship's bottom six and only two clubs scored fewer goals away from home. By way of contrast St Andrew's was something of a fortress, a 44-point haul was the fourth best record in the division.

Difference-maker? This could be a breakthrough year for young Danish striker August Priske. His first Blues goal came on the final day of last season at his father's former club Portsmouth, and he has regularly found the net in the warm-up games this summer. Priske has bulked up over the break putting some meat on his 6ft 5in frame. Over a full season, the 22-year-old may just prove to be a 15-goal plus striker.

Birmingham unlikely to get Osman back - Davies

Blues striker Priske 'has taste' for Championship

Andy Bayes, BBC Radio Lancashire

Key ins: Jayden Fevrier (Stockport), Sam Morsy (free)

Key outs: Sondre Tronstad (out of contract), Ryan Hedges (released)

Expectations? The main objective is to avoid a repeat of last season's struggles. Rovers won only four home games at Ewood Park last term and improving that record will be crucial. Tony Mowbray believes the squad still needs more quality and is hoping to bring in further additions before the transfer window closes.

Strengths? The experience gained from successfully battling relegation in two of the past three seasons should benefit the squad. Just as importantly, keeping key players fit and available throughout the campaign would significantly improve Rovers' chances of a more comfortable season.

Weaknesses? The squad still lacks Championship experience in key areas. Michael O'Neill highlighted this during his time at the club, and Mowbray has echoed similar concerns, although his primary focus is on adding quality. The Championship is a demanding league, and it can be difficult for inexperienced players to adapt quickly. The goalkeeping area is also of concern. Both Balazs Toth and Aynsley Pears are in the final year of their contracts. Toth could still leave before the window closes.

Difference-maker? Centre-back Tom Atcheson has begun the season as the first-choice option in defence. He turns 20 in September and is already being tipped for the top. The decision to hand him the number six shirt is a significant vote of confidence and it's likely he is already attracting interest from Premier League clubs.

'An amazing club' - Mowbray joy at Rovers return

Venky's 'want to help' with signings says Mowbray

Jack Dearden, BBC Radio Manchester

Last season: 5th in League One (play-off winners)

Key ins: Luca Stephenson (Liverpool), Ryan Hardie (Wrexham, loan), Gaizka Larrazabal (free), Lewis Brunt (Wrexham)

Key outs: Amario Cozier-Duberry (end of loan)

Expectations? The bottom line for me this season has to be about consolidating a return to this level, that's not to be confused with a lack of ambition, but a reality check. Bolton are more than capable of providing a few upsets and having a successful season, but they must find their feet early.

Strengths? Having had previous experience of the Championship Steven Schumacher is fully aware of what's needed in terms of performance and the value of an improved squad. It appears that they'll be operating on one of the divisions lowest budgets, which is why close season recruitment could be they key - a search which has been accelerated in the last few days, with eight new arrivals at the time of writing - and I'd suggest at least one more, possibly two on the way.

Weaknesses? Up front is ultimately where the main focus could fall. The ratio of opportunities created to goals scored is the main area for improvement - easier said than done admittedly, but no one suggested it was going to be straightforward, not many things are with Wanderers.

Difference-maker? Hardie - arguably his best spell of goalscoring came when he was with Schumacher at Plymouth. He could be a player to make a big difference to Bolton.

Bolton sign Wrexham defender Brunt

Bolton sign defender Larrazabal on two-year deal

Key ins: Lorent Tolaj (Plymouth), Dom Ballard (Leyton Orient), Sam Tickle (Wigan), Lisav Eissat (Maccabi Haifa), off the pitch Michael Skubala and James Ellis.

Key outs: Radek Vitek (end of loan), Ross McCrorie (Rangers), Mark Sykes (Millwall).

Expectations? More positive than they were at the end of last season but fairly realistic. It's been a big summer of change at Ashton Gate off the pitch, with James Ellis coming in as sporting director and Michael Skubala as head coach. With eight new signings and a bit more money spent than many fans were expecting, there's genuine optimism that things could change at City for the better and they could finally be genuine promotion contenders. But with so much change, that might take a bit of time.

Strengths? City have a strong looking set of centre-backs and central midfielders if they can keep them fit. At times last season it was last man standing, particularly in defence, but the additions of Eissat and midfielder Gibson Yah should help with that. If Jason Knight, who is also out of contract next summer, follows Max Bird in leaving before the window closes, they'll certainly need replacing.

Weaknesses? The signings of Tolaj and Ballard, who were among the best players in League One last season, has got City fans excited about their forward options for the first time in a long time. Both have good scoring records, but have never played in the Championship before. There are reasons to believe both will adapt well, but for now that still remains a question mark. As does the amount of time it will take the whole squad to adapt to a different style of football under Skubala.

Difference-maker? Tolaj certainly looks like he could be a cult hero at Ashton Gate with his all-action displays (and goals), but Yu Hirakawa is perhaps the most interesting. The Japanese winger helped Hull City to promotion to the Premier League on loan in the second half of last season. He couldn't find a place in the Bristol City squad as successive managers have played without genuine wingers. But with that changing under Skubala, he could be just the man they need for a team that has struggled to create chances against good defensive teams in the last few seasons.

Michael Skubala: New Bristol City manager on club's aims

Skubala wants 'quick, exciting football'

Andy Bayes, BBC Radio Lancashire

Last season: 19th in Premier League

Key outs: Maxime Esteve (Leipzig), Jaidon Anthony (Brentford), Luca Koleosho (Paris FC), Florentino Luis (Ipswich).

Expectations? It's still too early to make a firm judgement on Burnley's prospects. The Clarets have earned promotion from the Championship in each of the past two seasons they played in the division, both times reaching 100 points or more. They made bouncing straight back to the Premier League look easy. This summer, though, there is still plenty of business to be done before supporters and pundits can get a clear picture of what Burnley might achieve.

Strengths? Burnley have several players with a point to prove. Aaron Ramsey joined the club for a significant fee three years ago but has struggled with injuries. If he can stay fit, he could feel like a new signing. Mike Tresor failed to make a major impact under Burnley's previous two managers, but there is hope new head coach Nicky Hayen can help him rediscover his best form.

Weaknesses? The biggest concern is the possibility of losing more key players before the window closes. Zian Flemming is one to watch. The forward has been linked with a return to the Premier League and would be a difficult player to replace. Hayen has made it clear that any player who does not want to be part of his plans can leave, provided the club receives the right offer.

Difference-maker? Marcus Edwards could be a key figure this season. The attacker made a positive impression after arriving during the second half of Burnley's promotion-winning campaign in 2024-25. Many fans felt he was not given enough opportunities in the Premier League last season, and the Championship could provide the perfect stage for him to show his quality on a regular basis.

Walker targets instant Burnley top-flight return

'Vomitory' stairwell approved for Burnley FC stadium

Last season: 2nd in League One (promoted)

Key ins: Nathan Trott (Copenhagen), Jack Moylan (Lincoln)

Key outs: Ryan Wintle (MK Dons)

Expectations? Survival will be first priority for head coach Brian Barry-Murphy, who has brought life back to the club with his exciting style of football. If the Bluebirds can start the season strongly a top-half finish would mark a successful return to what is an extremely competitive Championship.

Strengths? The Cardiff squad is filled with young talent, many of who came through the academy. Under Barry-Murphy they have been allowed to express themselves and last season it worked wonders, bringing an excitement to the club not seen in many years. The pace at which they play and the freedom allowed by Barry-Murphy will see Cardiff carry a threat against any opposition.

Weaknesses? Strangely it feels as if Cardiff's biggest strength is also their biggest weakness. At present there are only three players in the Cardiff squad over the age of 30, and on occasions last season they showed signs of naivety - the likes of which will see you get punished in the Championship. On paper a few signings with significant Championship experience would not go amiss, but Barry-Murphy has stuck to his guns so far and that is unlikely to change anytime soon.

Difference-maker? The young talents of Dylan Lawlor, brothers Rubin and Joel Colwill and Cian Ashford will all have a significant role to play, but if Cardiff are to have a successful season they need goals, and all eyes will be on striker Yousef Salech. Despite being relegated to League One, the powerful Danish striker scored eight goals in 20 Championship games two seasons ago and netted 15 goals last campaign before a nasty neck injury saw him sidelined. If he is fully fit once more he will be a handful for any defender.

Moylan scores debut winner as Cardiff beat Swindon

Barry-Murphy has 'incredible hunger' to improve Cardiff

Key ins: Ivan Mesik (Heracles), Billy Koumetio (Dundee), Karlan Grant (West Brom), Danny McNamara (Millwall), Millenic Alli (Luton).

Key outs: Luke Berry, Lyndon Dykes, Macaulay Gillesphey, Karoy Anderson, Jayden Fevrier, Harry Clarke, Luke Chambers, Conor Coady

Expectations? Another season of trying to steer clear of danger.

Strengths? Charlton's defensive structure. It was more apparent at the start of last season rather than the end but they did keep a decent amount of clean sheets.

Weaknesses? Both fashioning and taking chances. The Addicks were among the lowest scorers in the division last term.

Difference-maker? Karlan Grant. Returned to the club in the summer and Nathan Jones will hope he will add more bite and quality to that attack.

Charlton sign Kenya midfielder Ouma

Charlton sign Republic of Ireland winger Alli

Key ins: Bobby Clark (Salzburg), Sam Szmodics (Ipswich)

Key outs: Liam Thompson (Mansfield)

Expectations? The collapse of the proposed takeover brought an abrupt end to hopes of significant new investment and a major transfer boost. For now, much rests on the final weeks of the transfer window. The current squad has quality but lacks depth, making further additions essential if Derby are to fulfil ambitions of challenging in the top half of the table.

Strengths? The outlook for the season has changed considerably in a short space of time. Derby possess a strong spine, with goalkeeper Jacob Widell Zetterstrom providing reliability at the back, captain Lewis Travis entering his first full season at the club after an injury-free pre-season, and Carlton Morris offering a focal point in attack if he can recapture the form he showed before injury last term.

Weaknesses? The Rams remain short in several positions, including both wide areas, full-back, central midfield and in attack. Finding players with proven Championship pedigree is rarely straightforward, and Derby's recruitment team face a challenging few weeks.

Difference-maker? Bobby Clark is likely to be one of the players to watch this season. At 21, he has the talent and potential to become one of Derby's most valuable assets. Patrick Agyemang is not expected to return until January following the injury that ruled him out of the World Cup, but his comeback could feel like a new signing midway through the season.

Eustace glad 'drama is over' after Derby takeover collapse

Derby 'off market' as takeover deal collapses

Rob Makepeace, BBC Radio Lincolnshire

Head coaches: Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw

Last season: First in League One, champions

Key ins: Andrei Coubis (Universitatea Cluj), Tanto Olaofe (Charlton, loan), Mason Melia (Tottenham, loan)

Key outs: Jack Moylan (Cardiff), Michael Skubala (head coach, Bristol City)

Expectations? Survive! When you haven't been at this level in over 60 years, just being able to stay up will be an achievement. It's going to be tough for the Imps with them expecting to have the lowest budget in the league. However, like they did last season when they blew League One away with not the biggest budget, City will be hoping to upset the odds once again.

Strengths? It's been a summer of little movement so the core of the squad which helped them achieve promotion remain and the continuity will help. They have a number of players like Tendayi Darikwa and Adam Reach who've done it at Championship level. The appointment of two head coaches might have raised a few eyebrows, but Chris Cohen and Tom Shaw are highly thought of in the footballing world and what might seem a risk might turn out to be a masterstroke.

Weaknesses? It's been a quiet window for City but between now and the end of August you would expect a few more faces to come through the door.

Difference-maker? After a difficult first season, goalkeeper George Wickens played a major part last season and signed a new contract over the summer. Through developing his game with goalkeeping coach David Preece, Wickens could be one of those English goalkeepers who suddenly finds himself in the spotlight in the coming years, just like Lincoln's former loannee Carl Rushworth.

Lincoln defeat Derby to progress in Carabao Cup

Lincoln sign Spurs' Melia on loan and retain trio

Last season: 5th (lost in play-off final)

Key ins: Will Lankshear (Tottenham), Sebastian Berhalter (Vancouver Whitecaps)

Key outs: Hayden Hackney (Everton), Dael Fry (Birmingham)

Expectations? After narrowly missing out on promotion last season, Boro expect to give it another good go this time around. The expanded play-offs are an absolute must for Kim Hellberg's side. Expectations were raised last season and Coventry's title win shows promotion doesn't always have to be beyond teams without parachute payments.

Strengths? Boro were defensively sound last season and brilliant at closing out games in which they scored first. Hellberg's style of play impressed opposing managers and fans alike and at its best is capable of blowing teams away.

Weaknesses? Last season's big problem was Boro's inability to break down teams who decided to sit deep and gift them possession. That led to a run of two wins from the last 10 games of the season which saw them drop out of the top two with the finishing line in sight. Boro hope the addition of Lankshear and Kyle Joseph up front will provide the ability to batter the door down if attempting to pick the lock fails.

Difference-maker? Will Lankshear. Boro have paid big money for an out and out number nine while it's hoped USA international Seb Berhalter continues the form that saw him shine for his country at the World Cup. In defence, Adilson Malanda was an outstanding addition during the second half of last season. Boro need his partnership with Alfie Jones to give them the platform to go out and dominate games.

Lankshear strikes on debut as Middlesbrough beat Wrexham

Middlesbrough sign USA midfielder Berhalter

Key ins: Kyrell Lisbie (Peterborough), Lyndon Dykes (Charlton)

Key outs: Billy Mitchell (Sheff Wed)

Expectations? After reaching the Championship play-offs for the first time in over two decades, the ambition will be for Millwall to challenge again. The fanbase is realistic, as there are many wealthier teams also going for promotion. However the way they dismantled so many reputations last season has shown what can be achieved.

Strengths? Manager Alex Neil is a huge asset. Not only does he seem to understand the club and the fan base – not everybody does – but he also has a great deal of experience in managing teams who win promotion. His know how could once again prove essential in those season-defining moments.

Weaknesses? Neil has received consistent backing from the Berylson family who own the club since he arrived and this summer has seen more investment to make the team as competitive in the Championship as possible. However, they will be up against teams with much larger budgets and that could, in the end, be a deciding factor. But it won't be for the want of trying.

Difference-maker? Millwall have been searching for a proper goalscorer for years. If Josh Coburn can replicate the form he showed for parts of last season – and remain injury free – then he could be that added ingredient that will give them an extra edge.

Jensen saves four shootout penalties as Millwall beat QPR

Millwall sign Scotland's Dykes on one-year deal

Chris Goreham, BBC Radio Norfolk

Key ins: Andre Brooks (Sheffield United), Sam Field (QPR), Darlin Yongwa (Lorient), Bruno Alves (Cruzeiro, loan).

Key outs: Shane Duffy, Emi Marcondes (end of contract)

Expectations? Cautious optimism is the overriding mood around the Norwich fan base. Only three teams won more Championship points in the second half of last season so there is real hope that Philippe Clement can pick up from where he left off, helped by having a full pre-season with the squad.

Strengths? Continuity. Norwich City have looked in good shape since Clement inherited a team that seemed destined for League One last November. The previous two summers have seen the head coach change and a series of signings from different foreign markets. The quieter, calmer close season this time is being seen as a positive.

Weaknesses? Injuries. Clement was frustrated last season by the number of players who were regularly sidelined. It's led to the club making a host of appointments in its sport science and fitness department. However they have lost winger Ali Ahmed to an ACL injury that means he's set to miss the entire season. Kellen Fisher, Jovon Makama and Lucien Mahovo are all likely to miss the opening weeks.

Difference-maker? Makama looked like a superb prospect after arriving from Lincoln last summer. He scored 13 goals before his season ended prematurely in February. Australian World Cup striker Mo Toure scored 10 goals in 12 games after signing last winter, including two hat-tricks. He made it 11 in 13 with a goal just 40 seconds into the Carabao Cup win over MK Dons. Andre Brooks has looked the part in pre-season, too.

Norwich confirm ACL injury for Ahmed

Norwich thump MK Dons in Carabao Cup

Key ins: Rocco Shein (Fredrikstad), Marko Milovanovic (Almeria), Abu Kamara (Hull City)

Key outs: Andre Dozzell (DC United, free)

Expectations? The ambition is to steer clear of the relegation battle. However, despite already spending around double what they did last summer, Pompey's budget remains modest and any improvement on last season's finish of 18th should be considered a fine effort.

Strengths? Josh Murphy and Abu Kamara have the potential to be a very exciting pair on the flanks, although both were injured for the majority of last season. Terry Devlin came on leaps and bounds last season and it's a surprise no one has tried to prise him away this summer. Adrian Segecic's tally of 11 goals in his debut season was impressive.

Weaknesses? Injuries hit Portsmouth hard last season and while that's something every team can expect, Pompey don't have the depth in quality to cope without key players. There's reasons to be encouraged by the new arrivals but there's very little Championship experience between them. Gone are the days of clubs naively thinking they can turn up at Fratton Park and easily win. Teams take Pompey very seriously at home and the Blues have struggled to break down sides who sit back against them.

Difference-maker? A fit and firing Josh Murphy is one of the best players in the Championship. Injuries ruined his last campaign and he's unlikely to feature in the season opener. But if he can re-find the form of two seasons ago, it's hard to see Pompey getting relegated. They are a different proposition with him playing.

Portsmouth move for midfielder Ceesay breaks down

Portsmouth should fear no one this season - Adams

Andy Bayes, BBC Radio Lancashire

Key ins: Alfie Devine (Tottenham), Delano Burgzorg (Middlesbrough, loan), Jusef Erabi (Genk, loan).

Key outs: Ben Whiteman (Wrexham)

Expectations? Preston North End are expected to make further significant additions to the first-team squad before the transfer window closes. The club has already spent a record £6m on Alfie Devine and if North End can strengthen in the way they hope, supporters will be aiming for a repeat of last season's strong first-half, but without the dramatic decline that followed after the turn of the year.

Strengths? North End have invested heavily in a new playing surface at Deepdale after the state of the pitch became a major issue last winter. It's cost north of £1.5m to make the required improvements. The previous surface made it difficult to play the style of football Heckingbottom wants and the club will hope the new pitch provides a platform for a more consistent campaign.

Weaknesses? Squad depth remains a concern. Several influential loan players have returned to their parent clubs or moved elsewhere, while experienced figures such as Robbie Brady have departed. Lewis Dobbin and Harrison Armstrong, in particular, leave sizeable gaps to fill, while Daniel Jebbison's departure also reduces Preston's options in attack.

Difference-maker? Devine is Preston's record signing and arguably their standout player. He impressed during his loan spell from Spurs last season and, having now joined permanently, there is every reason to believe he can take his game to another level. That said, he will need more quality around him if both he and the team are to reach their full potential.

Ten-man Preston beat Huddersfield on penalties in cup

Preston loan Burgzorg for the season

Key ins: Calum Ward (Motherwell), Pierce Charles (Manchester City, loan), Boy Kemper (NAC Breda, free), Tariq Lamptey (Fiorentina, free), Glen Kamara (Rennes), Dennis Cirkin (Sunderland, free)

Key outs: Steve Cook (Wycombe), Sam Field (Norwich) Paul Nardi (end of contract), Isaac Hayden (end of contract). Manager Julien Stephan's number two Alou Diarra also left over the summer.

Expectations? Hopes appear to be quite high after a promising transfer window and pre-season. Can QPR bridge the gap against the higher spending teams in the division, because that is what it will take to reach the top eight. Progress will be a top-half finish but if they start well and have better luck with injuries then maybe they can push on further.

Strengths? The fact that manager Julien Stephan has a season under his belt in the Championship should help, along with him being able to shape the squad more to his requirements.

Weaknesses? QPR conceded 73 goals last season. Only beleaguered Sheffield Wednesday conceded more across the season. Stephan has to sort this out if they're going to be challenging further up the table this season.

Difference-maker? I have a hunch that Rumarn Burrell could go well with a fair wind. He's got a lot of the qualities a forward requires to be successful in the Championship so if he stays fit and, crucially, if he gets good service, I think he could be a big hit.

QPR sign former Sunderland defender Cirkin

QPR boss Stephan signs new deal

Andy Giddings, BBC Radio Sheffield

Key ins: Romelle Donovan (Brentford, loan), Matt Doherty (free), Kalvin Phillips (loan)

Key outs: Gus Hamer (Coventry), Andre Brooks (Norwich)

Expectations? Expectations are lowering with each passing day in the transfer window. It not a shock that key players have been sold, but it hasn't helped the mood of an increasingly frustrated fanbase that's growing concerned about the lack of clarity from the boardroom.

Strengths? Sheffield United have some excellent players, with many proving with the Blades that they can mix it with the best in the Championship the season before last. Getting the best out of those players again is one of manager Chris Wilder's stated challenges this season. Having Wilder at the helm, and under a longer contract, is a major plus point after the failed experiments of the previous summer

Weaknesses? At the time of writing, strength in depth. They currently need two centre-backs, a midfielder and two left sided players, one of whom will be seen as a direct replacement for Gus Hamer. There is pressure on the owners to provide that otherwise the Blades will be trading their way out of the promotion picture.

Difference-maker? Hamer's replacement (pending) and a fit again Michael Cooper in goal. He's up there with the best keepers in the division.

Sheff Utd re-sign Man City's Phillips on loan

Hamer rejoins Coventry City on 'long-term' deal

Adam Blackmore, BBC Radio Solent

Last season: 4th (expelled from play-off final)

Key ins: Divin Mubama (Man City, loan), Cyle Larin (Mallorca), Daniel Peretz (Bayern Munich)

Key outs: Ross Stewart (Swansea, free), Shea Charles (Fulham)

Expectations? Southampton's players and head coach have made it clear that they want automatic promotion

Strengths? So far in the window Southampton have kept a large core of the players who went 21 leagues games unbeaten at the end of last season, and also permanently signed two key players from that squad who were on loan, in Cyle Larin and Daniel Peretz.

Weaknesses? Man City striker Divin Mubama has been brought in on loan to replace Ross Stewart. He has huge potential but after five goals in 20 starts before injury at Stoke, needs to show he can deliver over the course of a Championship season.

Difference-maker? Most fans would say Brazilian winger Leo Scienza is the difference-maker, and I wouldn't disagree. Barring a big club coming in with a stupid bid before the window shuts, Scienza will be giving full-backs nightmares all season.

Fulham sign Charles from Southampton for £30m

Key ins: Ethan Galbraith (Swansea), Djibril Soumare (Braga), Svante Ingelsson (Sheff Wed), Josh Griffiths (West Brom)

Key outs: Ashley Phillips (end of loan)

Expectations? The club's hierarchy has been clear. They expect to be competing for a play-off place this season.

Strengths? Stoke's good start to last season was built on a solid defence and Viktor Johansson's outstanding goalkeeping. Maintaining that solidity whilst adding more attacking efficiency is the key to success for the Potters.

Weaknesses? A lack of attacking threat outside of the goals and assists Sorba Thomas can provide. Stoke don't have a prolific striker and the rest of the squad has yet to prove it can contribute enough goals to make up for that.

Difference-maker? Young centre-back Luke Graham will take time to adapt following his summer move from Dundee but he's left-footed, robust and happy to step out of defence and has shown enough of his potential already to indicate he could turn into a very good player over the next year or two.

No hard feelings for Matos before Galbraith reunion

This season 'feels different' for Stoke - Robins

Key ins: Elijah Just (Motherwell), Joseph Opoku (Zalte Waregem), Tiago Parente (Benfica, loan), Ross Stewart (Southampton, free), Stephen Welsh (Celtic, free), Moussa Yeo (RB Salzburg)

Key outs: Cameron Congreve (Westerlo), Ollie Cooper (Notts Co, loan), Liam Cullen (Leicester), Ethan Galbraith (Stoke), Sam Parker (Wycombe, loan), Ricardo Santos (Sheff Wed)

Expectations? Not for the first time in recent years, Swansea head into a new Championship season hoping they can improve on a mid-table finish by mounting a genuine play-off push. With transfer questions still to be answered – particularly surrounding Zan Vipotnik – it is difficult to judge exactly how strong Swansea are. But after a second successive summer in which they have shown ambition in the market, the club's owners will be looking for progress after a second successive 11th-placed finish in May.

Strengths? Vipotnik, the Championship's top goalscorer last season, was Swansea's key man up front, while Ethan Galbraith was another top performer alongside left-back Josh Tymon and goalkeeper Lawrence Vigouroux. With Galbraith gone and Vipotnik's future uncertain, Swansea will need some of their new recruits to step up. Following Vitor Matos' appointment last November, Swansea played a pressing game which was particularly effective at home. Given his history working alongside Jurgen Klopp, Matos' commitment to the press is unlikely to change.

Weaknesses? Matos will be keen to improve his team's away record, given that a few more results on the road would have made a big difference last time around. Should Vipotnik move on, Swansea will be left looking to Adam Idah – who endured a tricky first season at the club – and new recruit Ross Stewart to carry the baton up front. Swansea's weakest department last season was out wide, an issue they have attempted to address by spending significantly on the likes of Joseph Opoku and Moussa Yeo.

Difference-maker? He has not been around long, but 21-year-old Ghana winger Opoku looks a player with the physical qualities to thrive in the Championship. Academy product Filip Lissah, meanwhile, seems set to become a first-team regular at Swansea for the first time after the classy defender impressed while on loan at Falkirk last season.

Swansea suffer heavy Burgess injury blow

Why three is no crowd for Swansea boss Matos

Geoff Doyle, BBC Three Counties Radio

Key ins: Federico Ravaglia (Bologna), Iker Bravo (Udinese), Omar Traore (Udinese), Jordan Zemura (Udinese).

Key outs: Giorgi Chakvetadze (Udinese), Nestory Irankunda (Sporting)

Expectations? The Watford board and owner Gino Pozzo would hope to be involved in a promotion challenge like they were last season until the final six weeks. For many fans - and this correspondent - expectations are lower. Watford ended the season dreadfully (failed to win in their last eight games) finishing 16th. Recruitment has been slow to say the least, so a mid-table finish seems most likely.

Strengths? Watford still have plenty of talent within their ranks with Othmane Maamma top of that list, although it would be no surprise to see interest in him before the transfer window shuts. The Hornets also still have Kwadwo Baah, who needs to re-discover his form and Rocco Vata who was hampered by injury last season, plus Edoardo Bove, who should be better having had a full pre-season.

Weaknesses? The spine of the team is a real concern as it stands. Watford have just two recognised centre-backs. Most clubs would have five. Signings (probably loans) will come in but they will have to integrate into the team and have an immediate impact (under a new head coach) which is never easy. Central midfield appears light with Imran Louza's future still up in the air. And upfront, the Hornets have two young centre forwards who are not quite at Championship level. Watford need to make some quality signings, quickly.

Difference-maker? Maamma is the standout player. The naturally gifted attacker can play left or right and is destined to play at the top level. Great balance, silky touch, game intelligence, and scores goals Maamma looks like one who will keep getting better and better. Hopefully, he will be with Watford for the season. Lesser known is young attacker Amin Nabizada is set for a break-out season.

Watford sign goalkeeper Walker from Bradford

Bola spares Watford's blushes against Crawley

Key ins: Barney Stewart (Falkirk), Jimmy-Jay Morgan (Chelsea, loan), Conor Townsend (Ipswich), Matt Ingram (Oxford United), Felix Horn Myhre (SK Brann), Rabby Nzingoula (Strasbourg)

Key outs: Jed Wallace (Bristol City), Karlan Grant (Charlton), Josh Maja (Le Havre), Daryl Dike (Orlando City), Josh Griffiths (Stoke).

Expectations? A massive improvement on last season, hopefully. The club inexplicably flirted with relegation to League One, but James Morrison rescued them with a 10-game unbeaten run. He now has the job permanently and, with two extra play-off spots on offer, that should always be the aim for a club the size of Albion. Achieving that is a different conversation, though, and with a younger, developing squad, a top-half finish would at least be a positive sign of progress.

Strengths? Morrison's miraculous rescue act was built on defensive solidity. He deployed a 4-4-2 formation, which is rare in the modern day, and players played in positions they were comfortable with. The team kept seven clean sheets in their final nine games, but also increased entries into the opposition penalty area thanks to advancing full-backs, so it was far from dull. Hopefully that organised intensity continues.

Weaknesses? Shots increased under Morrison, but turning chances into goals was a problem over the course of the previous campaign. Only four teams scored fewer than the Baggies, and two of them were relegated (Oxford and Sheffield Wednesday). Main striker Aune Heggebo bagged nine league goals in his debut season in England, so the Norwegian will want to improve on that, but he needs help. Spreading goals across the whole team is a must.

Difference-maker? Jimmy-Jay Morgan has scored five goals in pre-season and looks promising, but having not played in the second tier before, and after bigging up Isaac Price in this article last summer, I'm reluctant to put that pressure on the young forward's shoulders. Horn Myhre is a complete newbie to English football, but at 27 and having played in European competitions, he should be able to handle any expectations. I'm excited to see how the midfielder fares after being dubbed Brann's 'most important player' by one Norwegian journalist I spoke to. If he adapts quickly, he could play a pivotal role.

Return after 16-month absence 'amazing' - Townsend

West Brom sign Strasbourg midfielder Nzingoula

Head coach: Nuno Espirito Santo

Last season: 18th in Premier League

Key ins: Manor Solomon (Tottenham), Joel Veltman (Brighton, free), Keiber Lamadrid (Deportivo La Guaira)

Key outs: Mateus Fernandes (Tottenham), Crysencio Summerville (Al-Hilal), Freddie Potts (Club Brugge), Callum Wilson (Brentford, free), Adama Traore (released), Lukasz Fabianski (released)

Expectations? Anything less than automatic promotion will feel like an underachievement for a club the size of West Ham. If they manage to go up via the play-offs, it would still be considered job done, albeit not the preferred route. Failure to bounce straight back to the Premier League would be a failure.

Strengths? It is hard to look past the fact Nuno Espirito Santo has stayed at the club. The Portuguese is an excellent manager with top level pedigree and experience of winning the Championship with 99 points in 2017-18 at Wolves. West Ham have also still retained a competitive core and can lean on the prolific output of England international Jarrod Bowen.

Weaknesses? Off-field issues with an ongoing ownership tug of war could unsettle the club and may yet still impact West Ham's business in the transfer market before the window closes. Losing high quality players such as Fernandes and Summerville will inevitably lower the overall level of the squad and the Hammers must plug those gaps effectively.

Difference-maker? Perhaps the most obvious difference-maker in the entire division is of course Bowen. With 131 goal contributions in 228 games for West Ham since the start of the 2021-22 season, he is not only their best player, but probably the best player in the Championship.

Will West Ham bounce straight back up?

Quiz: How much do you remember about West Ham's 2011-12 season?

Last season: 20th in Premier League

Key ins: Raul Jimenez (free), Kieran Trippier (free), Rafiki Said (Standard Liege)

Key outs: Joao Gomes (Aston Villa), Tolu Arokodare (Ajax, loan), Matt Doherty (released)

Expectations? By the sound of Molineux last Friday, when over 21,000 were there for the Carabao Cup tie, fans have let bygones be bygones and start the new season with high hopes of an immediate Premier League return. All but the youngest Wolves fans have spent enough time in the Championship to know that the high hopes of mid-August can become brittle by September, but it is not difficult to make a case for Wolves achieving automatic promotion. As long ago as February, new executive chairman Nathan Shi was telling fans of an "18-month objective to ensure Wolves is a Premier League club by the 2027-28 season". Last Friday you could sense, for the first time in a long time, optimism in the stands that they really could.

Strengths? There are several players proven to have Premier League quality – Raul Jimenez and Kieran Trippier foremost among them – or with a fine past record in the Championship like Adam Armstrong, whose signing last January was taken as the first major move towards building a serious second-tier side. Last season was awful but some of the players who held their heads up and had been expected to move do not appear – for now – to be clamouring to leave. The positive choices of Jimenez to return and Andre to stay, when both could surely have found opportunities at higher levels in England or overseas, suggest that a core spirit of unity can exist, a powerful emotion in a demanding Championship programme.

Weaknesses? There are obvious questions. What if the exodus has not been cancelled, just delayed? If any of the seniors who appeared unwanted in May but now might be important components of the Championship challenge do go, can the club do better than last summer's flawed recruitment? Is there enough defensive strength apart from Ladislav Krejci, whose pre-season was limited after the World Cup? Will either of the club's two international goalkeepers end up staying, and if not can another senior keeper be found? The answers to these questions may not become clear until 2 September.

Difference-maker? This time last year, Mateus Mane's abilities were well-known only to those who nurtured him at Rochdale or closely studied the form of Wolves' youth teams. But several months before his departure, Vitor Pereira had identified Mane as a future star, and under Rob Edwards the teenage forward was given the first opportunities to demonstrate that ability. Arguably there were too many opportunities for his age and his season faded out, but he had already shown enough to be the focus of fans' hopes for the future. Through pre-season he has appeared fresh, motivated and refreshingly well-grounded, as if appreciating that a strong Championship season could gold-plate his potential for a major future.

Quiz: How much do you remember about Wolves' 2017-18 season?

It's a new era, the past is the past - Peixoto

Key ins: Danny Imray (Crystal Palace), Ben Whiteman (Preston), Anthony Patterson (Sunderland)

Key outs: Paul Mullin (Rotherham), Jay Rodriguez (released), Andy Cannon (Fleetwood, free)

Expectations? There is no doubt that Wrexham want to be pushing for promotion, particularly having gone so close to securing a play-off spot last season. A top eight finish will likely be viewed as a success given the restructuring of the play-offs, although the Red Dragons will want to push for top six.

Strengths? The squad possesses some real individual talent, including Josh Windass and Callum Doyle, while Kieffer Moore's variety of talents up front make him a real danger in the Championship. Wrexham are also very clinical. Phil Parkinson's side outperformed their expected goals (XG) by 12.21 last season, more than any other second tier side. Maintain that ruthless nature in front of goal and the Red Dragons will have another strong campaign.

Weaknesses? They gave up plenty of chances and efforts on their goal last season. It took time for Parkinson to find a settled back three in 2025-26, and injuries at wing-back certainly didn't help the team's balance. The hope, and probably even expectation, is that Wrexham will improve defensively having had a year to acclimatise to the division.

Difference-maker? Danny Imray, who was the club's first signing of the summer, has the profile to slot in seamlessly on the right flank. The injury record of last season's first-choice wing-backs Liberato Cacace and Issa Kabore was poor, but Imray has chalked up 76 appearances during loan spells across the past two seasons combined.

'Big decisions' for Wrexham as Falchener targeted

Wrexham sign Sunderland goalkeeper Patterson

title: Titans & underdogs - League One club-by-club preview
description: BBC Sport correspondents assess the strengths and weaknesses of all 24 teams competing in League One this season.
fullText:
League One has some titans joining the fray this season.

Leicester City lifted the Premier League trophy a decade ago but now they return to the third tier for the first time since 2009, while Sheffield Wednesday are back to kick off a new era under brand new ownership.

But with such recent, rich history comes mammoth expectation and for the Foxes in particular, nothing else will do other than promotion.

While for a club like last season's League Two champions Bromley, who have already reached a new height in securing promotion to League One for the first time, the pressure is off.

Could this be another year of the underdogs?

Follow your League One club this 2026-27 season

Key ins: Dan Sweeney (Stevenage, free), Steve Seddon re-signing for the new season

Key outs: Omar Bugiel (Suzhou Dongwu, free)

What are the expectations heading into the season? Keep their heads above water, and keep improving.

What are the major strengths of the team to help them achieve that? Defensively the Dons can be tough to breakdown.

And what are the underlying weaknesses that could hold them back? Far too streaky, runs of wins will almost certainly be followed by a long barren drought.

Who's a player to look out for this season who could be a difference-maker? Marcus Browne - technically brilliant, he's a key man in all good things they do.

Adam Oxley, BBC Radio Sheffield

Key ins: Cameron McGeehan (Northampton, free), Sam Gale (Gillingham, undisclosed), Clayton Taylor (Newcastle Jets, undisclosed)

Key outs: David McGoldrick (Mansfield, free), Adam Phillips (Bradford, undisclosed), Eoghan O'Connell (Stockport, free)

Expectations? Daniel Stendel has been a popular choice, external to replace Conor Hourihane as head coach this summer. The German has returned to Oakwell hoping to repeat the success he achieved in his first spell when he guided the Reds to the Championship in 2018-19.

Barnsley have a limited budget as the owners aim to operate within their means. A top-half finish would feel like a step in the right direction for the Reds, but the fanbase - who have seen their side play in the second tier for the majority of the club's history - will expect the team to be at least knocking on the door of the play-offs.

Strengths? The focus has been on recruiting young, hungry players to Stendel's high-energy, high-pressing game.

Retaining key midfielders in Patrick Kelly, Luca Connell and Reyes Cleary, coupled with the youthful enthusiasm of the club's new signings, the majority of whom are aged 23 and under, will offer hope that Stendel can mould a team to at least cause problems for the more fancied teams in the division.

Weaknesses? The Reds have lost goals and experience this summer with last season's top three scorers David McGoldrick (18), Davis Keillor-Dunn (16) and Adam Phillips (11) all having departed Oakwell.

Returning midfielder Cameron McGeehan, who previously played at Oakwell in Stendel's first spell, is currently the only player in his 30s in the squad, and a lack of a few experienced heads has historically not served Barnsley well.

Difference-maker? Patrick Kelly is likely to be crucial to any success that Barnsley achieve this year. The 21-year-old got better and better throughout his first campaign with the Reds and ended the season as a full Northern Ireland international, scoring his first goal for his country against France just before this summer's World Cup.

Norwood is now the oldest player at the club and has been handed the armband too. He might be 35 but still has the quality to unlock any defence.

Weaknesses? McNulty has never managed in League One but insists he is "completely ready" for the step up. However, it feels likely it could be a season of transition, as he attempts to implement his methods. Expect lots of possession - but do they have enough match winners?

Difference-maker? On-loan Manchester City goalkeeper Oli Whatmuff has followed McNulty to Edgeley Park from Rochdale, following his heroics at Wembley. He certainly doesn't lack confidence and has been called "a future England number one" by his manager. No pressure.

Josh Watton, BBC Radio Manchester

Key ins: Max Power (Bradford, undisclosed), Sonny Perkins (Leyton Orient, undisclosed)

Key outs: Sam Tickle (Bristol City, undisclosed)

Expectations? It feels like heading into the unknown with Wigan. They have finished 12th or below for the past three seasons, fans see this as a huge underachievement.

Gary Caldwell has made his ambitions clear, he wants to put that run to an end and finish comfortably in the top half, I'm not sure if they have the squad to achieve this on paper, however Caldwell is an expert in working wonders with a lower budget.

Strengths? Max Power has returned to the Latics for a third time, he'll come in and add some much-needed leadership in the middle of the field, that seemed to be lacking last season.

Weaknesses? Firepower up front, Joe Taylor solved that issue last season but it was only a temporary fix. Their second top scorer last season came from midfield, Callum Wright chipped in with seven and he has also left the club after his loan ended. If they are to achieve their goals this season, they really need to solve their issues in front of goal.

At other end, Sam Tickle has been invaluable for Wigan ever since coming into the first team, I imagine having him in goal has saved them around 10 points a season. He has now moved on to Bristol City and leaves a huge gap which has been filled with Joe Walsh, who has huge shoes to fill.

Difference-maker? Sonny Perkins is the new number nine at Wigan and has a lot of weight on his shoulders.

Gary Caldwell has experience in getting the best out of forwards, turning them into 20 goal a season strikers. If he can work his magic again, Perkins may live up to the expectations which were placed on him whilst rising through the West Ham and Leeds United academy.

Sam Avery, BBC Radio Three Counties

Key ins: Conor Hazard (Plymouth Argyle, free), Sam Parker (Swansea City, loan), Silko Thomas (Leicester City, free), Cauley Woodrow (Luton Town, undisclosed), Emre Tezgel (Stoke City, loan)

Key outs: Will Norris (Salford City, free), Declan Skura (Walsall, loan), Fin Back (Released), James Tilley (AFC Wimbledon, loan), Alex Lowry (Motherwell, loan)

Expectations? Fans are generally enthused about the prospect of a full season under Michael Duff, given the upturn in form following his appointment last season. As a result, there is optimism that the play-offs could be within reach. Having said that, it looks like a much tougher League One than last season.

Strengths? Continuity from last season. Before the injuries to some key players in March, the Chairboys were on track for a really strong finish to last season.

Fred Onyedinma, Dan Harvie and Cauley Woodrow were some of Wycombe's top performers in that time and all signed new contracts - or signed permanently in Woodrow's case!

Weaknesses? At the time of writing, Emre Tezgel is the only out and out striker that the club have signed this summer, leaving a lot of pressure on him to fulfil the shortcomings from Wycombe's high expected goal rate last season.

But, the biggest challenge facing the club this season might be the stadium! The terrace has been partially closed for structural repairs, leaving fans concerned about the effect that could have on the home atmosphere.

Difference maker? The obvious pick would be Fred Onyedinma after winning Supporters' and Players' player of last season. But, Ewan Henderson might just be the one to look out for. He was playing well last season until a couple of injuries before the New Year, but has looked really sharp again during pre-season.

title: Can Chelsea go from 10th to title again?
description: With a new manager at the helm in Xabi Alonso, can Chelsea go from 10th to the Premier League title like they did a decade ago?
fullText:
Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League 10 years ago but incredibly were champions of England just a year later under new manager Antonio Conte.

After finishing in the same position last season, with no European football again and a new manager in Xabi Alonso, can the Blues repeat the feat?

Chelsea's Premier League record in 2025-26 is almost identical to when they finished mid-table under interim manager Guus Hiddink a decade ago.

With just one more goal scored and one more conceded, they finished with the same goal difference and just two points more than they did in 2015-16.

Few would have imagined back then that after finishing 31 points behind champions Leicester and below the likes of Southampton, West Ham and Stoke, Chelsea's players would be the ones lifting the Premier League trophy the following season.

After starting the campaign playing a back four, a 3-0 defeat at Arsenal in just their sixth game saw Conte switch his side to a back three. The impact was tremendous as they won their next 13 games in a row.

It's a tactical switch that the Blues could make this season as well under new manager Alonso, given that his Bayer Leverkusen side won the Bundesliga unbeaten in 2023-24 playing three at the back.

That incredible winning run gave Chelsea what proved to be an unassailable lead at the top of the Premier League, as they won 18 games more than in 2015-16 to win the title with 93 points.

Improving the club's points tally by a whopping 43 points again is undoubtedly a huge ask for Alonso's squad, given that it's the biggest points increase that any side has achieved to win the title in Premier League history (Leicester improved by 40 points the previous season).

But they may not need to. While Arsenal will likely mount a stronger title defence than Leicester, the Gunners' points tally last season was the second-lowest to win the Premier League since Claudio Ranieri's side 10 years ago.

The bar to become champions has dropped in the last couple of seasons from the dizzying demands of the Guardiola-Klopp era – where even 97 points wasn't enough in 2018-19 – so Chelsea might not need to reach the 93 that they achieved under Conte.

While Chelsea would still need to improve considerably to win the title, they were better than their lowly 10th-place finish last season suggests.

Based on their underlying expected goal numbers, Chelsea were the fourth-most dominant team in the Premier League (although they drop to fifth once penalties are excluded).

The problem was that Chelsea struggled to take their chances. They scored eight fewer goals than they should have, given the number and quality of shots they took – just 58 from an xG of 66.3 – with only Crystal Palace and Wolves worse finishers than them last season.

Bizarrely, the majority of that xG under-performance in front of goal came in just five games in March and April under Liam Rosenior.

Despite taking 73 shots worth 5.5 xG, the side lost five successive league games without scoring for the first time in 114 years – a run of defeats that saw Rosenior ousted as head coach.

Did Chelsea become bad finishers, was it simply a run of bad luck or was it something else? Whatever the reason, the Blues are unlikely to suffer such a sudden slump again this season.

Given where they finished, the Blues will not be playing in any European competition this campaign. While that's obviously something clubs the size of Chelsea seek to avoid, there are benefits to playing just one game a week.

Since the so-called 'Big Six' – Arsenal, Chelsea, Liverpool, Man City, Man Utd and Tottenham – all finished in the top six of the Premier League for the first time in 2010-11, nine of their sides have had no European football to play, with Chelsea and Tottenham set to join that list this season.

All but one have finished higher in the Premier League, with sides moving up five places and taking 16 more points on average than they did the previous season.

While Conte's Chelsea obviously took full advantage by winning the title, Liverpool also came very close to lifting their first Premier League trophy in 2013-14. After finishing seventh the season before, an absence of European football saw them take 23 more points but they ultimately fell just two short behind champions Manchester City.

Manchester United also took advantage of playing once a week last season by taking 29 more points than they did in 2024-25 to finish third, although there was a lot of room for improvement after finishing 15th with just 42 points the season before.

Chelsea's transformation under Antonio Conte was incredible, but there's another title-winning side that can match it – Alonso's Bayer Leverkusen in 2023-24.

After taking over as manager in October 2022 with the club in the relegation zone, Alonso led them to a sixth-place finish that season with 50 points – the same tally as Chelsea in both 2015-16 and last season (although Bundesliga sides play four fewer games).

Then in his first full season in charge, Leverkusen incredibly took 40 more points in 2023-24 – just three fewer than Conte's Chelsea did – to win their first-ever Bundesliga title without losing a single game.

Only two sides in Premier League history have finished outside the top three one season and won the title the next – Leicester in 2015-16 and Chelsea a year later – so the Blues repeating such a feat would be remarkable.

But with a team better than they looked last season, the benefit of no European football and a new manager that's already pulled off a miraculous transformation at one of his former clubs, it's certainly not impossible.

title: Boxer Colon dies 11 years after brain injury in fight
description: Prichard Colon, who suffered a severe brain injury during a 2015 fight, dies aged 33, his father Richard confirms on social media.
fullText:
Prichard Colon, who suffered a severe brain injury during a 2015 fight, has died aged 33, his father Richard confirmed on social media.

Colon collapsed in his changing room after the fight with Terrell Williams, during which he complained about repeated punches to the back of his head

The Puerto Rican had suffered a brain haemorraghe and after having an operation to reduce brain swelling he was placed in a coma for 221 days.

Colon lived the rest of his life in a vegetative state - unable to walk or talk - and required 24-hour care.

"Good morning, my people. I regret to inform you of the departure of my son Prichard from this earthly world," Richard Colon wrote on Facebook.

"Now he is in a better world. I did everything possible to fulfil his wish, his dream of bringing him on vacation to Puerto Rico as he so desired, but it couldn't be done.

"Thank you for so many years of love and prayers. As much as you can, please keep us in your prayers."

Colon was undefeated in 16 fights with 13 wins by knockout before facing Williams in Fairfax, Virginia.

During the light-middleweight contest, Colon appeared to be struck in the back of the head on several occasions and Williams was deducted a point for illegal blows.

Colon was later docked two points for a low blow and was knocked down in the ninth. Believing the fight was over, Colon's corner team removed his gloves and he was disqualified.

His parents filed a lawsuit seeking more than $50m (£37m) in damages against the ringside doctor and promoters connected with the fight.

That lawsuit remains unsettled.

Colon, who was born in Florida but moved to Puerto Rico aged 10, showed great promise as a teenager and won national titles in two weight divisions.

He also boxed at the Brazil pre-Olympics with the aim of winning a spot at the 2012 Games in London, but lost in the quarter-finals and moved into the professional ranks for his debut in 2013.

"A true warrior in every sense of the word, Prichard left us with profound lessons about life, resilience, and our sport," the WBA posted on X.

In 2021, Colon was named an honorary WBC world champion by president of the sanctioning body Mauricio Sulaiman.

"Eleven years of fighting like a true champion receiving the unconditional love from your mother Nieves, your dad and so many friends who cared for Prichard Colon you will never be forgotten," Sulaiman wrote on X.

title: Swiatek answers internet critics with Toronto title
description: Iga Swiatek secures her first WTA title of the season with a straight-set victory over Elena Rybakina in the final of the Canadian Open.
fullText:
Iga Swiatek secured her first WTA title of the season with a straight-set victory over Elena Rybakina in the final of the Canadian Open on Thursday.

The six-time Grand Slam winner was cheered on by the crowd in Toronto as she beat world number two Rybakina 6-2 6-3.

Australian Open champion Rybakina struggled in the opening set and made 12 unforced errors, while Swiatek, 25, broke the Kazakhstan player's serve twice - and saved two break points of her own.

In the second set, Rybakina, 27, was unable to break world number eight Swiatek, and the Polish player clinched her 26th career title in one hour and 15 minutes.

"It means so, so much to me because the past months were not easy," said Swiatek, who will return to the top five in the rankings following her first Canadian final victory.

It has been a tough campaign for Swiatek, who will be looking to claim her first Grand Slam title since her dominant win in the Wimbledon final last year when the US Open starts later this month.

She advanced to the quarter-finals of the Australian Open in Melbourne in January but was beaten by eventual champion Rybakina. In the French Open and this year's Wimbledon, she only reached the fourth and third rounds respectively.

She appointed Spaniard Francisco Roig, who previously worked with Rafael Nadal and Emma Raducanu, to her coaching team in April.

Swiatek says it can be challenging to contend with external criticism while searching for her best form.

"I'm really happy that I kept focusing on growing, changing my game a little bit, improving despite all the opinions that many people have about me every day on the internet," said Swiatek.

"It's not easy to deal with all of that."

Rybakina led 2-1 in the second set before Swiatek won five of the final six games to end the match as champion.

Runner-up Rybakina had one ace and four double faults, hitting just 13 winners and making 23 unforced errors in total.

"I tried my best but it wasn't enough," said Rybakina, whose previous three matches went to three sets.

Meanwhile, Great Britain's Katie Boulter earned her first career win at the Cincinnati Open by defeating American Katie Volynets 7-5 0-6 6-4 in the first round.

After sealing her first victory since June, 30-year-old Boulter will face Wimbledon champion and sixth seed Linda Noskova in the second round.

In the men's final, fifth seed Ben Shelton secured back-to-back Canadian Open titles with a 6-3 7-6 (7-4) victory over fellow American Brandon Nakashima.

The all-American final was the first at ATP Masters 1,000 level since Andy Roddick beat Mardy Fish in Cincinnati in 2003.

Shelton is the first Canadian Open winner since Novak Djokovic in 2016 to win the tournament without dropping a set, and also the first player since Rafael Nadal in 2019 to successfully defend the title.

The 23-year-old arrived in Montreal following a disappointing run of results, suffering a first-round exit at Wimbledon, a second-round defeat at Roland Garros and managing just one win across his first four Masters 1,000 events of the season.

"To play the way that I've played this week, to go through this draw without dropping a set, I think it speaks a lot to the work that I've been putting in, but it speaks a lot to my mental toughness," Shelton said.

title: What's going on with Southampton boss Eckert's FA probe?
description: While Southampton felt the full force of the EFL's disciplionary powers at the back end of last season, Spygate is far from over with the future of Tonda Eckert still uncertain.
fullText:
While Southampton felt the full force of the EFL's disciplinary powers at the back end of last season, Spygate is far from over with the future of head coach Tonda Eckert still uncertain.

Saints' Championship campaign gets under way on Sunday and it still remains to be seen how Eckert, who was charged last month by the Football Association (FA), will be punished.

BBC Sport has been told the FA hearing is likely to be held in mid September.

Once the result is known, and with the possibility of an appeal to follow, Southampton will be a significant way into their campaign.

Eckert was charged with misconduct by the FA on 22 July for his role in the Spygate scandal that led to Saints being kicked out of the Championship play-offs in May after admitting they spied on three clubs last season.

The ongoing investigation is looking into who participated in the spying and assessing the culpability of those who knew it was happening.

BBC Sport also understands that the intern involved, Will Salt, is set to be appointed to a permanent analyst role with the club since the controversy.

Saints owner Dragan Solak revealed to BBC Sport in early June that he would not sack Eckert and that he was deserving of a second chance.

That could be taken out of his hands if the German coach is handed a lengthy ban, and it could happen in the midst of the Championship season.

The EFL opened its investigation into the spying allegations before the play-off semi-finals and charged Southampton with spying on 8 May.

Eleven days later Southampton learned their fate and were thrown out of the play-offs and given a four-point deduction for this season.

Unlike in the EFL case, which needed to be resolved in order to complete the play-offs, the FA process has allowed Southampton more time to submit evidence in support of their case.

When Southampton finally present that case it will be approaching four months after the FA began its investigation.

The Championship will pause for three weeks between Monday, 21 September to Tuesday, 6 October for the international break - but whether Southampton will learn the outcome by then is not yet known.

In short, it will depend on how long the ban is.

Eckert is only contracted at St Mary's until the end of the current season, and a significant sanction could force the club to look elsewhere for a new head coach.

Group technical director Johannes Spors provided some insight into the board's current thinking during the recent BBC Radio Solent Southampton FC fans' forum.

Spors has held his position since 2025 and played a key role in handing Eckert the permanent job as head coach in December last year.

"It all depends on what the outcome is as there are so many uncertainties of how this could look like," Spors said.

"There is nothing too concrete at the moment, we're really focused on the here and now and if there is something that we have to deal with then we will deal with it.

"In the back of my mind and in the office we do speak about different scenarios to be prepared for but I still hope for a positive outcome."

Southampton were preparing for a number of possibilities on their pre-season tour.

During one friendly Eckert watched the game from the stands, and later told the club's media: "Let's hope we don't need it," when asked about managing the game away from the technical area.

If Eckert were to be banned by the FA, there is no guarantee this would only prevent him from being on the touchline.

"At the moment I'm honestly very positive looking into the next weeks and we have some ideas in mind," Spors added.

"There was some discussions earlier about how Tonda watched one of the pre-season games from above [in the stands] and we have to think into different scenarios like this."

Throughout the Spygate process, members of the Southampton board have maintained a stance that they feel the punishment does not fit the offence committed.

Parsons echoed those feelings at last week's fans' forum but has urged the club to move on, revealing that Eckert has now been asked to "focus on football".

After initial disapointment from within the Southampton dressing room, the whole saga appears to have lit a fire inside those Saints players who missed out on playing in last season's play-off final.

Club captain Jack Stephens felt that Spygate had brought the group together, while midfielder Flynn Downes said the squad have a chip on their shoulder heading into the Championship season.

A similar mentality seems to have been adopted by some Southampton fans, who were chanting "we'll spy when we want" in their Carabao Cup opener against Colchester on Saturday.

On the other hand, some supporters raised concerns at the recent forum about season ticket prices increasing for the current campaign despite all that happened in May.

Parsons explained that the extra cost was being reinvested back into the stadium to increase the fan experience but said he appreciated people's frustrations.

While Eckert has had time to think over the summer about his actions and last season's events, the coach revealed he has been proactive during his time off, as well as cooperating with the FA's investigation.

His only prior work in senior football before the Southampton job came through 15 months as the number two at Barnsley, and three years as assistant boss at Italian club Genoa.

The 33-year-old recently revealed he had used the summer period to sharpen up his knowledge of the EFL's rules and reach out to some fellow professionals in the game.

"I've had a lot of support very quickly from the owner, sporting director and the players, but then also over the summer from lots of managers in the game, and that's helped me a lot over the summer," Eckert said in his pre-Watford news conference.

"I used the summer to not only go through the 131 rules but also to connect with some managers that have been in the game for much longer than me and managers that have much more experience than myself across national teams and club football.

"One is for the rules and regulations and the second that is even more important is the culture that's behind that, I've done that through many conversations with English managers, not just in football but other sports too."

After last weekend's 2-0 cup victory away at Colchester, Southampton start their Championship campaign at Vicarage Road on Sunday when they take on Watford.

This weekend Eckert's opposing manager will be Italian Alessio Dionisi, who he previously came up against during his time at Genoa while Dionisi was at Sassuolo.

title: 'We have to be better' - why Man City can't dwell on double
description: Manchester City have bolstered their squad this summer - but will they have enough to defend their Women's Super League crown?
fullText:
Manchester City won their first Women's Super League title in a decade last season, adding the Women's FA Cup trophy to their cabinet for good measure.

However, with Arsenal strengthening this summer and Chelsea hoping to bounce back after a disappointing campaign, can City stay at the top in 2026-27?

City are also being chased by ambitious clubs lower down the table as London City Lionesses and Tottenham have made waves in the transfer market and Brighton have been on the rise under manager Dario Vidosic.

City have bolstered their squad with the additions of England internationals Beth Mead and Niamh Charles - but will they have enough to defend their crown?

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

What are the key dates for the women's football season?

City were crowned champions with a game to spare and a six-point gap to second-placed Chelsea last season.

It ended Chelsea's six-year dominance and was City's first major trophy under manager Andree Jeglertz in his debut campaign in England.

No Champions League football, a squad stacked with quality and the ability to keep key players fit proved vital - but what did the players learn?

"How to become champions," captain Alex Greenwood told BBC Sport.

"We had come very, very close to doing it in previous years but just couldn't get over the line. Last season, a lot came together."

There will be new challenges this season as City return to European football meaning a busier fixture schedule.

The squad will be tested more, though they were boosted by top-scorer Khadija Shaw's decision to sign a new contract, avoiding a potential switch to Chelsea.

The arrivals of England duo Mead and Charles has added depth but City lost Brazilian forward Kerolin to Barcelona.

Elsewhere, Spain full-back Ona Batlle and England midfielder Georgia Stanway have joined Arsenal, London City Lionesses have signed two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas and Tottenham have improved their frontline with the additions of Kirsty Hanson and Shekiera Martinez.

But Greenwood is not fazed by others and says the message to her team-mates remains the same, though they need to keep improving.

"Continuity is important, culture is important and the language that you use is important. When you hear the same thing often, it becomes a norm," she added.

"You act like a champion and perform like one. We all locked into that last year and were fully committed.

"This season, I'm not going to say 'do the same again' because I don't think that entitles you to win the league. People improve, teams improve and we will improve.

"We will have to change things slightly and be better but continue to do the things that we did really well last season. That would be my message... and to enjoy it."

Inside Man City's WSL title-winning season

Unmasking the coach plotting Man City's quest for a domestic double

Investment at clubs outside the WSL's top four makes for an exciting season ahead with deeper competition across the league.

City will have to be wary of their traditional rivals, but also of clubs looking to upset the usual order such as London City Lionesses, Tottenham and Brighton.

However, Greenwood does not think they need to be looking over their shoulders.

"I think the reaction is from the teams who have tried to get into the top four and haven't quite got there," said Greenwood.

"It's amazing though. I love seeing players come to this league and want to test themselves. In my opinion, it's the best league in the world in women's football.

"I don't think any game you play in the WSL is easy. We'll see when the season starts how things look. I concentrate on this team and where I'm at."

It is another big year for Greenwood, who is hoping to help England go far at the Women's World Cup in Brazil next summer.

She is used to the big stage having won back-to-back European titles with the Lionesses but Greenwood says lifting the WSL trophy as captain taught her things.

"It was those big moments of pressure - I was interested to see how I would handle those situations," she added.

"I've been in winning teams where we've won trophies but I was captain last season so it did feel a little bit different in terms of responsibility.

"I really enjoyed it. I tried to embrace it as much as I could. I relied on people to help me in situations where I felt I needed it and I don't think that's a bad thing.

"I'm not perfect and I don't have all the answers just because I wear the armband. I did learn a lot about myself. I learned to enjoy it along the way too because it gets tense!"

title: Hasan hits Bangladesh's first century in Australia
description: Tanzid Hasan Tamim becomes the first Bangladesh cricketer to score a Test century in Australia as the visitors continued to dominate on day two in Darwin.
fullText:
First Test, Darwin (day two of five)

Australia 198: Smith 71; Mahmud 6-55

Bangladesh 351-6: Tanzid 101, Shanto 84, Mominul 49

Tanzid Hasan Tamim became the first Bangladesh cricketer to score a Test century in Australia as the visitors continued to dominate on day two in Darwin.

The opener, playing in just his second Test match, hit 101 off 197 balls as Bangladesh closed on 351-6, a lead of 153.

"I can't describe it in words, but it was very special for me," he said. "I love to play in these conditions, the pitch is getting better and better."

Hasan began the day on 32 with Bangladesh 96-1, having bowled Australia out for 198 on day one after the hosts won the toss.

The 25-year-old put on 102 for the second wicket with Mominul Haque, who was dismissed by Josh Hazlewood for 49 before lunch.

Tanzid then put on 93 with captain Najmul Hossain Shanto as Australia toiled in stiflingly hot conditions at the Marrara Oval.

His innings finally came to an end when he drove a Nathan Lyon delivery to Mitchell Starc at long-off during the afternoon session.

Australia rallied with three quick wickets with the new ball after tea, but Mehidy Hasan Miraz and Hasan Mahmud put on an unbeaten 43 before stumps to keep Bangladesh on top.

Australia have never lost a home Test to Bangladesh, only losing once to the Tigers in six previous Tests - at Mirpur in 2017.

This is the first of a two-Test series.
